stem: In a world with no taxes and perfect capital markets, a firm's unlevered cost of capital is 9%, its cost of debt is 5% and its debt-to-equity ratio is 0.6. According to Modigliani-Miller, its cost of equity is closest to:
explanation: MM Proposition II without taxes: r_e = r_0 + (r_0 - r_d)(D/E) = 9% + (9% - 5%)(0.6) = 11.40%.

rationale.A: Incorrect. 10.68% applies a (1 - t) factor of 0.7, which belongs only in the version with corporate taxes.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 7.40% starts from the cost of debt (5% + 4% × 0.6) instead of the unlevered cost of capital.

stem: An all-equity firm is worth 800 million. It issues 300 million of perpetual debt and uses the proceeds to repurchase shares. Under Modigliani-Miller with a 30% corporate tax rate and no costs of financial distress, the value of the levered firm is closest to:

rationale.A: Correct. The present value of the perpetual tax shield is 0.30 × 300 = 90 million, added to the unlevered value.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 800 million is the MM result without taxes; with taxes the tax shield adds value.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 1,100 million adds the full amount of debt; issuing debt to buy back shares only changes the split of value, apart from the tax shield.

stem: According to the pecking order theory, a profitable company that needs to fund a new project will most likely prefer, in order:
options: new equity, then debt, then retained earnings
retained earnings, then debt, then new equity
debt, then new equity, then retained earnings
explanation: Because of information asymmetry, issuing securities sends signals. Internal funds send none, debt sends little, and new equity can signal overvaluation, so it is used last.

rationale.A: Incorrect. This reverses the pecking order; new equity is the least preferred source.
rationale.B: Correct. Internal funds first, then debt, then new equity as a last resort.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Internal funds come first because they avoid issuance costs and negative signals.

stem: Under the static trade-off theory, which company is most likely to have the highest optimal debt ratio?
options: A regulated utility with stable cash flows and large tangible assets
A software start-up with negative cash flow and mostly intangible assets
A biotech firm whose value depends on the outcome of drug trials
explanation: The optimal debt level balances tax shields against expected costs of financial distress. Stable cash flows and tangible, collateral-friendly assets keep distress costs low, supporting more debt.

rationale.A: Correct. Low business risk and tangible assets mean low expected distress costs, so the optimum is reached at higher leverage.
rationale.B: Incorrect. Negative cash flows leave no taxable income to shield and intangible assets give little collateral, so distress costs dominate.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Binary, uncertain outcomes create high distress risk and high indirect bankruptcy costs.
